Mr. Chairman, there are a few matters to which I should like to direct a little special attention. We must not lose

Supply-Health and Welfare sight of the necessity and urgency for doing something about blind pensions. The minister has mentioned this, and I know she has some problems in working out a solution in conjunction with the provinces. However, I believe she has enough drive to bring it to a head and do something more for the benefit of blind people, as has been already done on old age security.
I also want to speak for a few minutes on the question of disability pensions. For far too long the definition of a disabled person has been much too strict. Actually this philosophy of a disabled person having to be in a wheelchair or lying in bed is ridiculous in this day and age. It should be related to his ability to have or to get any type of employment.
In this connection there is another point which we encounter in practice over and over again. Quite often a disabled person is a married man, and his wife goes out to work because the disability allowance is quite insufficient to keep the household. However, once she earns more than $1,980 a year, or $165 a month, she is in trouble. That is ridiculous, because quite often she has to pay carfare or drive a motorcar to get to her place of work. She has to buy food, clothes, pay for rent and fuel, and look after the furnishings in the house. It is ridiculous for officials to penalize people simply because they are showing thrift.
When I was home last week end a case was drawn to my attention of a mother who had two children going to high school. These two were over 16 years of age, and she had a third child coming into that age bracket. Through you, Mr. Chairman, I say to the minister of health that the promise of the Liberal party to continue family allowances as long as children are at school should be implemented at once. I think there is general agreement that they said they would extend it to the age of 18 years, and as a matter of fact the Minister of Justice stated in the house that the government had a plan, which he thought was a pretty thorough going one, and that it would be introduced in due course.
There is a little urgency about this in view of the fact that the cost of living has increased. It should be remembered that boys and girls are being kept longer at school not only upon the insistence of the parents and the department of education which exhorts the parents to keep them there, but also on the advice of the federal government which says the young people should continue at school to learn the necessary skills so that they will not be unemployed. Surely we cannot have it both ways.
Mr. Chairman, I wanted to dwell for a little while on the question of the conference


that is being held here next Monday. I know and appreciate that the Minister of National Health and Welfare has taken a very sympathetic attitude toward this matter, but I wonder whether she or the ordinary person realizes the great importance of this conference. I recall that when I went to medical school 35 years ago, cancer of the lung did not have to be considered at all and was not looked for. We were looking for tuberculosis and other things on the X-ray plates. When a radiologist looks at an X-ray plate today, he looks at it very carefully to see if there is any evidence of cancer. From 1899 to 1919, if my memory is correct about these years, in the University of Minnesota they reported only three cases of cancer of the lung. In the year 1919, at that same university hospital, they reported only one case. In the years 1949 to 1952 they reported over 264 cases. We must bear in mind in this connection, Mr. Chairman, that generally speaking very few cigarettes were smoked prior to the first great war. Since that war there has been a gradual step-up year by year in the number of cases of lung cancer which have occurred in the United States. The increase in the number of cases of cancer of the lung has been paralleled by the increase in the consumption of cigarettes, and in the year 1960 there were 37,000 people who died of cancer of the lung in the United States.
It is true that in proportion to men, not many women have died of cancer of the lung, but I hope this does not start the minister back on the road to destruction, because there has been a marked increase over the years in the number of women who have developed this disease. To demonstrate the seriousness of this situation I say to you, Mr. Chairman, that out of every 100 of these cases of lung cancer that are diagnosed, within five years 95 of them are dead, regardless of the type of treatment carried out. Therefore it follows that there is only one form of treatment, and that is prevention. When we look at the record and all the surveys that have been made, we realize that to all intents and purposes those who do not smoke do not contract cancer of the lung. I want to go a little further, Mr. Chairman, and say that we can consider a religious group, the Seventh Day Adventists, who do not smoke or drink, and we find that to all intents and purposes they never contract the disease of cancer of the lung.
I have illustrated that there is no cure for this disease, and in Canada today more people are dying of cancer of the lung-and this is leaving out coronary diseases and all the other things; and there are about double the number of deaths in the coronary field-from

among those who smoke than is the case with non-smokers. Today more people are dying in Canada every year of cancer of the lung than from traffic accidents, bad as they are. Therefore the conclusion one must reach is that the cigarette plays a very definite part in causing cancer of the lung. I have emphasized to you, Mr. Chairman, that the only treatment for this disease is prevention. This prevention must go back to the boys and girls between the ages of 14 and 17 in our high schools today, because I think it has been fairly well proven over and over again that if a boy or girl has been smoking for two years, they have acquired the habit. To illustrate the seriousness of this problem I would point out that it is estimated that over 400 boys and girls start smoking cigarettes every day in Canada.
I know the minister is very well aware of most of these facts, but I want to impress upon her that to carry out a policy of prevention in this regard you must have the good will and the support of everybody across this nation. There is no question as to what the findings will be, because they have been proven over and over again; but to get that good will and support you must have the backing of the men and women across this country. You must have the support of the press, of members of parliament, and of all the people generally. So I ask the minister- and I know all the difficulties, and I know that if it were easily done she would have agreed to do it long ago-to very carefully consider obtaining a larger room, if it is at all possible, so that the press, the members of this house and the Senate, and other interested people may come into this meeting and hear first hand the story of tobacco, cigarette smoking and cancer of the lung. Through you, Mr. Chairman, I would ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare to give this question most careful consideration.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to see if I can raise this debate to a scale that is a little less depressing than that achieved by the hon. member who has just spoken. I do not mean that I disagree with what he said, but there are other things that we must consider. I would like to see if I can imbue the Minister of National Health and Welfare with some common sense thinking about a national health plan. Realizing that the Liberals have been promising this since 1919, I am going to try to give them some reasons for implementing it now.
I like to feel that in our modem society the blessings of good health and the advantages of many new discoveries and developments are not only for those who can financially afford them. I like to feel that when a new
Supply-Health and Welfare discovery comes about, it will be available to anyone who is in need of it and not just to anyone who can afford it. The development of a national health plan is so that this may come about. Popularly, Mr. Chairman, today this is known as medicare. It has been said that everyone is adequately cared for by our present system. I do not even consider this is a system, much less that it is adequate. I admit that a great many people are cared for in one way or another, but certainly not properly, by present standards. It is my considered opinion that there is a large group of people who are medically indigent. I am not referring to those people who are now receiving charity, but those whose budgets do not allow them to receive adequate care and, in many instances, no care at all. These people will let things go until they reach serious proportions, rather than run up a medical bill. These same people, when they do come to the office, are often inadequately treated either because they do not get the required prescription, for financial reasons, or the doctor substitutes something cheaper than the best treatment, something they can afford to buy.
These are the ways in which I consider that people receive inadequate care. We cannot change the ways of people who are incapable of budgeting for an illness. I do not believe that people are asking for charity, nor do I believe in the degradation that a person must suffer in order to receive some sort of medical care in the event of illness. There are some who would forgo medical treatment rather than receive it under these circumstances. A properly planned comprehensive national health plan would remove this barrier of having to receive charity in order to obtain medical care because everyone would be paying for this in accordance with his ability to pay and consequently would be financially responsible. To this extent, the stigma of charity would no longer exist. As a practising doctor, I feel an important barrier would be removed. Our medical freedom to treat patients is limited by financial considerations which are, medically speaking, entirely irrelevant.
Another financial barrier is that of indebtedness of the patient to the doctor. It provides a tremendous psychological barrier between doctor and patient. Certainly, a doctor's judgment is hampered by the realism of the debt that exists between them. When I refer to a national health plan, I am referring to an all-inclusive completely comprehensive national medical insurance plan. This is one that not only covers doctors' services but includes dental care, medication, eye glasses and appliances. Anything less than this in a

Supply-Health and Welfare national plan is inadequate. Private insurance plans are never this comprehensive. None of them include dentistry and only a few of them include partial drug payments. All of them are covered with exclusion riders, waiting periods, exceptions, omissions and fine print. It often takes a lawyer to interpret them and one often feels that to collect from them is committing a felony.
I cannot see how a national plan would cause an increase in expenses. Medical care is now costing X number of dollars, and the only increase would be the cost of administration and the proper care of those inadequately cared for now. Part of the cost of administration would be offset by the removal of profits now enjoyed by the private insurance companies In other words, a national insurance plan would simply level expenses, as does any insurance plan.
I turn now to the opposition to medicare. The main opposition to medicare is purported to be the doctors. The doctors have stated that the people would abuse the plan. In my opinion, this only proves that people are being inadequately treated now because they do not want to burden themselves with financial expenses they cannot afford. Must we use financial inadequacy as a deterrent to medical care? Doctors are represented as being dedicated people, dedicated to the care of others, and yet all their arguments against medicare have to do with their own, private feelings. I should like to quote from an article in the Globe and Mail of May 21, 1963. This is a short joke which reads as follows:
Fred: What did your doctor tell you?
Al: He told me to cut down on my smoking, try to walk a mile a day, and to be sure to write a letter to my member of parliament against medicare.
Doctors belong to many associations such as the Ontario Medical Association, the Canadian Medical Association, and their colleges of physicians and surgeons in the various provinces who are their licensing bodies. These bodies lay down the rules and laws that govern the ethics, behaviour and economics of the medical profession. Doctors who do believe in a government sponsored compulsory medical health plan are afraid to go against this norm that is set down by the association to which they belong, and say what they truly believe. Is this the true purpose of an elected body that is supposed to portray the wishes of all its members?
I have seen letters from doctors in Saskatchewan, and after reading them I was actually ashamed to admit I was a member of this profession. Am I idealistic when I state that I always thought doctors belonged to a profession that served sick people and

that this was their prime function? I realize that economic problems and factors are important and that doctors must live, but must they appear to be interested in the welfare of people and yet, at a time of crisis, show a selfish interest in their own welfare? Medicare eliminates a doctor's economic problems. I do not believe the associations that represent the medical profession truly express the feelings of the members, but rather their own feelings. The impression that is given to the public is that these bodies do truly express all the doctors' views, and I feel that this is a false impression. It is not my intention to deprecate the medical profession, especially since I am a member myself, but I do feel that the misrepresentation should be known.
There would be no harm in this if it did not involve the health of the working man and his family. Health is a necessity for making a living and the responsibility for this lies with the medical profession. These doctors are hard working and most are truly devoted to their duties, but in many instances are misrepresented by their own elected governing bodies. Is it fear of these bodies that prevents us having a properly run, government sponsored all-inclusive medical health plan? There are no private plans that are adequate, as was proven by work done in Hamilton at the Steel Company of Canada. The Ontario Medical Association is stating that up to 70 per cent of the people have adequate medical care. This is truly deceptive because only 47.2 per cent of people have some form of health insurance. It now only remains to show the inadequacy of present plans.
P.S.I. is considered to be the best of the private plans, and it covers 18 per cent of the population. An exhaustive survey was conducted in Hamilton by the department of political economy of the University of Toronto with the help of the steelworkers union. By comparing P.S.I. with a profitmaking plan, P.S.I. was found to be the best, and yet P.S.I. paid only 23.5 per cent of the average total health costs of the families who subscribed to it. The people who have P.S.I. are better off than others who have one of many profit-making plans that cover only 12.9 per cent of the average family's total health cost. These plans are riddled with escape hatches for the insurance companies in the event they are paying out too much to any one person. These policies may be cancelled at the whim of the company by refunding premiums, or exclusion riders may be attached after an illness in order to exclude the system involved or any future diseases which may develop. What kind of protection is this for anyone? What kind of

protection is this for a man who must earn a living for himself and his whole family? Surely, his illnesses are not self-inflicted so that he must be punished for them and then expected to go through the degradation of receiving charity.
Only 18 per cent of all Canadians enjoy the best kind of private plan available, and even these plans pay less than one quarter of the family's total annual health cost. The reason for this low figure is that none of them include dental care, eye glasses, appliances or drugs. The statistics are rather shattering when one listens to the propaganda of the Ontario Medical Association, the Canadian Medical Association and the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, who are the enemies of any national health scheme. These people tell us that it is a person's individual right to choose his own plan. Really, he has no choice except to select an inadequate private plan, to join the army or be admitted to a mental home, if he wishes to receive adequate care.
If the representative bodies of the medical profession can come up with a privately administered plan that gives the kind of coverage the British people enjoy, well and good. If they cannot, then we should get on with the business of a government sponsored compulsory health plan. You cannot manipulate statistics forever. Let the doctors and their associations either produce or keep the status quo, but let them stop hoodwinking the public. People are afraid they will not be able to choose their own doctor under a national health plan. This is not so. Actually, conditions would be the same as they are now without the financial barriers between doctor and patient. Doctors would be paid for services rendered only, thereby maintaining the doctor's incentive to treat his patient. This fear or ignorance, and it must be realized that ignorance produces fear, prompted the Ontario Medical Association to produce a small booklet entitled, "Doctor, What About Medicare?" This booklet was circulated to every doctor in Ontario and is full of propaganda against government sponsored plans. Again, I ask, is this truly the feeling of the medical profession? This book was available at a slight cost for putting into doctors' waiting rooms for distribution to patients, so that this propaganda would spread even farther.
I should like to quote also from an editorial in the Star Weekly of a few months ago. This editorial deals with the fear the doctors have about a government medical insurance plan. If the doctor's fear is that he does not want a layman dictating treatment for his patient, or want anyone to tell him the type of drug a patient needs, or the number of X-ray
Supply-Health and Welfare plates it is necessary to take, it is well realized that these are medical decisions and can only be made by qualified personnel. This editorial is summed up in this manner:
What Canadians want is a system that will provide all of them, rich and poor, with the medical care they request. They do not want to bilk the doctors. They merely want to make sure that every citizen gets medical attention when he needs it. not as a matter of charity, but as a matter of right. This, we think, is a principle with which most doctors would agree.
I should now like to go into the success which other countries have enjoyed in this direction. We happen to be distinctive in that with the United States we are the only two countries in the world which have no government sponsored medical health plan. Great Britain has put in some of the most successful government sponsored health plans at a time of Great Britain's greatest austerity. It was, of course, the British Labour party that did this, at a time when it seemed almost impossible. Since 1953 Great Britain has had a Tory government, and yet no attempt has been made to remove this plan. As a matter of fact, recently the British Tory government instituted methods of improving some of the parts of the system.
A few months ago there was a panel consisting of general practitioners, specialists, and politicians who came over from Great Britain to the United States, and this panel was heard and seen over a nation-wide television network. The general concensus of all the panel was a complete satisfaction with their system, and the only thing they feared was the misrepresentation which the press have given us over here.
There are only two countries left in the world today that do not have some form of government medical plan-Canada and the United States. The ability of a country to provide these necessities to everyone is a reflection of the political and cultural status of a country. Our status cannot remain one of the status quo; we must advance and we must do so in a completely democratic way.
It has also been said that the quality of medicine would be lowered because of the increase in quantity. Even this is not so, as evidenced by a study on the Norwegian health plan. Two of the most universally accepted measurements of the merits of a given medical system are the infant mortality rates and the life expectancy at birth. The infant mortality rate in Norway is 20.5 per thousand births and in the United States it is 26.4. Norway ranks fourth in the world and the U.S. ninth. In the life expectancy figures Norway ranks best in the world with 71 years for men as against 66 for men in the U.S. Medical

Supply-Health and Welfare education in Norway is free, thereby producing opportunity for everyone with ability. The figures just given are not because there are more doctors per capita. In 1953 Norway had one physician for every 900 population, whereas the U.S. had one for every 760 population.
Other parties in Canada have made rather futile attempts to establish provincial health plans. The only one that has been established successfully and which is operating successfully at the moment is in Saskatchewan, where they have a partial medical health plan; they have provided doctors' care. Everyone knows there was a rather bitter battle over this scheme at the time of its inception, but even those doctors who were so stubborn and obstinate at that time are today of different mind. There was an article in last night's Ottawa Journal headed: "Battle lines on medicare blurring in Saskatchewan". I should like to read a small part of this article:
The battle lines drawn by Saskatchewan doctors and the C.C.F. government over the compulsory medical care insurance plan put into operation 16 months ago are blurring.
The tempered attitude of doctors, who once said they were unalterably opposed to compulsory medical care insurance in any form, is reflected in comments of Dr. E. W. Barootes of Regina, vice president of the Saskatchewan college of physicians and surgeons, who last year was an outspoken critic of the socialist government's plan.
"The profession hopes that these differences of view that exist can be ironed out and modifications made so that the plan will be acceptable," he said in an interview. "There are some pretty deep philosophical differences but we don't want to pick a quarrel".
I think that is a pretty good statement, coming from a doctor who opposed the plan so adamantly only a year and a half ago. The editorial continues:
Provincial health minister A. E. Blakeney says the possibility of changes in the plan is not excluded by the government.
"It is the government's view that the plan is operating successfully and will continue to operate successfully. It is obtaining a wide measure of public support and is beginning to gain acceptance among the medical profession," Mr. Blakeney said.
They also mention this, although it happened about two months ago:
In September, the government announced a 50 per cent reduction in one of the four levies that finance the $20,000,000 a year plan. Personal premiums were reduced from $24 a year to $12 for families and from $12 to $6 for individuals.
So as I say, despite objections at the time of its conception this plan is proving to be one of the most successful yet advanced. It makes me proud to be a member of the political party which was capable of putting forward the first successful plan on the North American continent.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is a pleasure for me to participate in the estimates of the

Department of National Health and Welfare. I well recognize that this department could be one of the most important departments of government. Throughout the years I have been very interested in the welfare and health of our senior citizens and youth, and for that reason my remarks will be confined to this subject.
First may I dwell on the welfare and health of our senior citizens, as we well realize that these people, along with the pioneers of our nation, have established and upheld many fine traditions in this great country of ours. When listening to the minister's speech on July 18, 1963 respecting the Canada pension plan, my first disappointment was that the government's promise during the last election of $75 a month to our senior citizens who meet the residence requirements of the old age security act would not come into effect at once. I can assure you that when talking to these senior citizens, such a delay was a real disappointment. With the higher cost of living they would have to be content to do without most of the necessities of life. As a director of Waterloo county's apartments for elderly persons, which are sponsored by the Royal Canadian Legion, branch No. 50, Kitchener, I well realize the necessity of such an increase. Our constant interest in and consideration of their welfare makes them feel that they are wanted citizens and not just a burden on mankind. Many of these people are first war veterans who, owing to their disabilities, have not been able to prepare for the future and are therefore unable to compete with other citizens who have the normal advantages. Such an increase, which should have been forthcoming some time ago, will give them greater security and an independent feeling in life.
Another situation we might well consider at this time is where a couple may be in receipt of old age pension, and death strikes leaving a burden on the survivor for debts incurred. Perhaps such pension of the deceased might be extended for a certain period to help the survivor to defray such expenses.
When speaking to our senior citizens I found much discontent over the price of drugs and medical prescriptions which generally appear too high for pensioners, especially those of low income. Surely some system could be devised where these necessities could be made available free to those below income tax level. In bringing forward this raise we also have an obligation to those citizens who are receiving old age assistance, blind and disabled allowances. Their future lives are in our hands. Humanitarian service extended to these people should be sincere and of most importance.

As I previously mentioned in this house on June 24, 1961 it is desirable that we give further consideration to those of our citizens reaching the retiring age of 65 years. These folk in many cases have not had the opportunity of providing for their future through superannuation or pension plans. Many of these people are on the unemployment list or were unable to have retirement postponed, and therefore are in financial difficulty at an age when they should be able to have some security other than just owning their own homes and a few belongings. It is an acknowledged fact that these citizens have played a prominent part in developing the economy of our country. I am sure that we, as hon. members of the house, along with the Department of National Health and Welfare, can devise some system to look after their financial needs at the retiring age.
Owing to improvements in medical care and otherwise, we have a greater population of people in the age group 70 or over, as well as those in the 65 to 70 year age group. These circumstances make our obligations much greater. Many fine improvements have been made in the Old Age Pensions Act. The previous government made the most beneficial improvement when they lowered the residence requirement from 20 to 10 years in regard to old age pensions. Another splendid move was that recipients are now permitted to take their pensions with them when leaving Canada on a permanent basis. I am sure that our senior citizens living outside of Canada or contemplating doing so for various reasons, are appreciative of such legislation.
My second thought concerns the fine youth of our country, but before expressing my observations on fitness and amateur sports, may I suggest that we who are parents should take a good look at our daily obligations with regard to assistance and guidance extended to them in their responsibilities as future citizens of Canada. Like all proud parents, we expect a lot of our younger folk, and we must do so if our young country is to fulfil its ambitions. However, we must not forget that they will only be able to shoulder their responsibilities in a manner consistent with the teachings and with the example which they will have received from us. To my mind, however, education in such a way is not related only to the three R's. It covers a much wider field. For one thing, good citizenship is required of all the individuals making up a nation, if that nation is to be strong and healthy. I am sure hon. members will agree with me that such education means developing in our children a strong sense of responsibility as individuals. But responsibility means work, and unfortunately too many of us have the natural tendency to leave it to
Supply-Health and Welfare the other fellow to do the job. The pass-the-buck or let-George-do-it policy has never been known to lead to great achievements. So, as I said before, let us teach by setting a good example first, and then by giving young people plenty of opportunities to assume responsibilities. They will make mistakes, as we have done, but they will learn, and in the process they will realize that they too have an important role to play in the aspirations of our nation.
With regard to fitness and amateur sports, I was interested in the remarks made by the Royal Canadian Legion's "Coaching Review" of June 1963, which had this to say:
A fresh mind is quickening the pulse of Canadian amateur sport these days, giving it new initiative, leading, eventually to its expansion and development in the light of current needs and standards.
As part of that initiative the Royal Canadian Legion has launched its sports training program, with particular emphasis on improving the coaching and performance of track and field athletics. For some years the Royal Canadian Legion of Waterloo, Ontario has made a great success of promoting the eastern Canada track and field events, along with events in other places across Canada, and some time ago I had the great pleasure of taking part in the opening of the Kitchener public schools track and field event where
6.000	children were in attendance and over
1.000	competitors took part. Much credit is due to this committee for its outstanding success. Such events mean healthier boys and girls. Members of the Legion, like other sports-minded citizens, believe that track and field, and indeed, all sports, should be enjoyed at the bottom level as well as the top level.
For years the Royal Canadian Legion has made tremendous contributions to the welfare of our youth in various ways, and recently acquired one of the world's greatest coaches, Mr. Geoffrey Dyson of England, to carry out their sports training program. I had the pleasure, last year, of attending this program in Guelph, Ontario, and recently I attended the clinic sponsored by the Kitchener recreational council at which time this gentleman was in charge and later was guest speaker at the luncheon. To hear this man and to see him in action is a real treat, and inspired over 100 men attending this event. No doubt, such action by the Legion in securing the services of such a distinguished gentleman can be attributed in no small way to the $5 million fitness and amateur sports program brought forward by the previous government and passed by parliament and the other place. I sincerely believe that the national advisory council, made up of outstanding sportsmen and representatives of every province, along
5024	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare with the superb coaching ability of Mr. Dyson, and men of similar ability will in five years or so put Canada in its rightful place in world sports activities, and more important, will develop generation after generation of young Canadians with healthy bodies and healthy minds.
I am pleased to see the minister take an interest in this sports effort, and I hope her future assistance may continue so that this fine program will expand to the point where our athletes may compete with the best in the world, and more important, where every Canadian youth may take part in order to develop a greater standard of fitness and a wider knowledge of sportsmanship, fellowship and friendship. I spoke a moment ago of Mr. Dyson. This great coach, who played a major role in developing in England a coaching elite second to no other country, and whose presence will have a profound beneficial effect upon Canadian coaches and athletes, mentioned that communities are interested in fitness for different reasons'- such as health, military efficiency, national regeneration, racial and personal self-esteem, social accomplishment, character building and aiding mental activity. No doubt all these reasons have been and are being presented in support of programs of physical activity.
Speaking of military efficiency, it is obvious that governments which use armed force as an instrument of foreign policy cannot allow fitness standards to fall beneath a certain level. Pushbutton warfare has certainly not eliminated the need of physically fit troops, and military standards are still higher than civilian standards. In some countries the fall in fitness reached a critical point. For example, in the 1959 Berlin crisis, the United States government had to reject 428 men out of every 1,000 called up, for lack of physical efficiency. This was almost double the rate of the second world war. It is well known that fitness has both political and international implications. Politically, national fitness and sports campaigns can help weld nations together, particularly the United States, Canada and other comparatively young countries where people have come together from different backgrounds. This is very noticeable in my riding of Waterloo North where we have one of the largest cosmopolitan centres in Canada. This district has turned out some of the finest hockey players, golfers, football players, etc., and is certainly interested in fitness and amateur sports.
The former minister of national health and welfare, speaking in 1962, mentioned a growing spirit of nationhood. We find many countries in the world bringing forward huge expenditures for sports and fitness. France


is one of these, and her aim is to check the flow of youth from country to town. Communist countries in particular have long recognized the political importance of sporting success. This is also true in England where in 1954, the British foreign office sent Roger Bannister to the United States immediately after his first four-minute mile.
We realize that today the best performers in sport are new ambassadors in a political sense, particularly with regard to sport, for sport is international and inter-racial. We realize that sports can also be used as an outlet for the natural tendency and desire, so deep in human nature, to prove superiority, but we must remember that superiority can be won at too high a price.
Having followed the program of fitness and amateur sport since its inception, I want to congratulate the former minister of national health and welfare, his staff and the members of the national advisory council for the splendid efforts accomplished in these few short years. I realize that many Canadians expected this program to produce wonders in a very short time and I might tell the minister that I am sure many people may well think it should do the same in the next few years, but it is going to take ten or 12 years to bring the program up to the mark. Let us work together so that the program may achieve the desired success.
As we know, many grants have been made to deserving organizations. However, if the federal government is going to assist the great majority of our youth in Canada with regard to fitness and amateur sport, and if the opportunity for gifted athletes is to be increased, these things cannot be done merely by grants to national agencies interested in national and international sports competition. The framework through which better coaching as well as fitness can be encouraged by the federal government will depend upon provincial and municipal programs as well as the contributions of sports bodies. This is of the utmost importance.
Under such a program we need the cooperation of provincial and municipal departments of health, education, welfare, municipal affairs and others and through provincial governments we need the cooperation of municipal recreation departments such as we have at the present time in my constituency of Waterloo North where such co-operation has developed a combination of coaching and training to strengthen and extend fitness and sports programs for all our young people, which I hope will be exemplified in every part of Canada.
In my speech on September 22, 1961, I suggested that our three realms of activity could be:

1.	The provision of sports facilities, adequate playing fields, stadia, swimming pools, gymnasiums, tennis courts, and other training and competitive areas. These facilities would mean fitness for our youth.
2.	The provision of competent coaches, something that is invaluable to our youth.
3.	Direct financial aid to national organizations and teams representing Canada in international events.
The Legion has made a move in the right direction in the provision of coaches with their appointment of Mr. Dyson. The national advisory council, through the former minister of national health and welfare, has provided direct financial assistance to many worthwhile national organizations. Such a move has proven its worth, and from time to time I hope more grants will be made to associations which in turn will help their affiliates. I commend the minister for her recent grant to the Royal Canadian Legion and also to Father Bauer and his team from British Columbia, because it is of interest to me, as Father Bauer was born in my riding.
It has been suggested by well known sportsmen that at the present time we lack proper sports facilities such as playing fields, stadia, etc. Our future aim should be to improve such facilities so that our coaches in all sports will have modern buildings and playing fields strategically located in every province, where each province will have the opportunity of sharing in the cost of same.
For our physical fitness program many auditoriums could be used in our universities, colleges, schools, Y.M.C.A.'s, churches, etc..
These are some of my suggestions and thoughts, Mr. Speaker, with respect to a fitness and amateur sports program. I sincerely hope that the minister, along with her staff and the advisory council, will continue the splendid work undertaken by the former minister and those who assisted him. In this way we can look forward to a brighter future in fitness and amateur sports in Canada. As previously mentioned, we can put Canada in its rightful place in world sports activities and, more important, develop generation after generation of young Canadians with healthy bodies and healthy minds and a true understanding of sportsmanship, fellowship and friendship.

As for health insurance, we should take into account the fact that the Liberal government had advocated a hospital insurance plan and that during the years which followed, many difficulties had to be overcome with the provinces as well as with the hospitals throughout Canada.
One may think that such plans can be put into effect overnight but with due reflection, we realize that it is better to take all necessary steps and understand the situation before carrying out such plans.

If the hon. member for Lapointe wants to be a bit patient, I intend to go back to 1919 and show him that, as opposed to certain members, who have their rights as I have mine, I chose to remain in the Liberal party rather than try to form a new one which would never get anywhere.
Mr. Speaker, I was dealing with the problems we have been up against in trying to set up a hospital insurance scheme. First, there was the matter of hospital beds, then the agreement to be reached with the provinces, not to mention the number of nurses. We must realize that the hospital accommodation necessary to meet a situation such as the one created by the acceptance of a hospital insurance scheme required some preparation.
I can say, without running any risk, that the former minister of national health and welfare, the present Secretary of State for External Affairs, found a way, in 1945, to get the cabinet to agree to a general plan to expedite payment of the grant to the provinces and hospitals that wanted to expand in order to be ready for the day when the hospital insurance scheme would be implemented.
For the information of the hon. member for Lapointe, I will point out that it was a five-year plan. In 1950, the plan was renewed.

Supply-Health and Welfare Several hospitals in nine provinces took advantage of it and increased their facilities to be able to cope with the hospital insurance scheme.
Mr. Chairman, I should say in passing that in 1945-I was at that time a member of the provincial legislature-during the election campaign preceding the provincial election in Ontario, our leader advocated an insurance program. I myself campaigned in favour of an insurance plan with a nominal rate for each family.
However, the Conservative party in office at that time in Ontario opposed such a plan.
I do not blame them, and I do not say that they did wrong. The Conservative party was not ready yet to accept the idea of health insurance and throughout its election campaign it fought against the program advocated by the Liberal party.
Since the Conservative party had more members elected, it remained in power, of course, and did not establish any health insurance plan.
Therefore, from that year until 1957, the province of Ontario still refused to accept hospital insurance. It is only in 1957 that this province finally agreed to a hospital insurance plan. This goes to show, Mr. Chairman-I shall perhaps repeat myself in order to be better understood-that it might be argued that such things can be accomplished overnight but, all the same, they require years of preparation, because the government must take into account the expenses incurred through the establishment of those plans.
That is why I feel at ease to declare that those who readily repeat that the health insurance plan was part of the 1929 Liberal platform, forget to mention what the Liberal party has done-

Mr. Chairman, since 1927 the Liberal government managed to insert in the statutes of this country the pension with means test for needy people aged 70 and over. In 1940-I may be told that it is not health legislation- but it certainly has some effect on public health-in 1940, as I said, the Liberal party

enacted unemployment insurance. In 1944, family allowances were introduced. In 1945, there was the first phase of the national health scheme subsidizing hospitals desirous of enlarging their premises, in order to be ready for the day when the provinces would accept hospitalization insurance.
In 1950, came the second stage; the department of national health offered a program of grants to any hospital willing to avail itself of it.
In 1951, the Liberal government introduced the old age security pension without means test, for anyone having reached the age of 70 and over.
In 1951, a pension with means test was granted to needy people in the 65 to 70 age bracket.
In 1951, there was the pension for the blind.
In 1954, we had the pension for disabled persons.
In 1956-and there is another thing which you might say is not directly connected with health insurance or with the Department of National Health, but which certainly has some effect on the health of the unemployed-there was the contribution of 50 per cent to the provinces to assist unemployed people who were not protected by unemployment insurance.
In 1957, we had the hospitalization insurance act which was passed and entered into the statutes of this country though I admit, that it was later enacted by the government elected in June.
Now, we must keep in mind, Mr. Chairman, that when the pensions act was introduced, it only provided for $20 a month. Under the following Liberal governments, and keeping pace with this country's development, as well as with the needs of the beneficiaries, those pensions were gradually increased to $46 per month.
I shall give credit to the Conservative government for having granted two consecutive increases; but-and this was quite remarkable-always on the eve of some election.
As far as we are concerned, we just granted another $10 increase-

his cabinet, had decided to grant these allowances only up to the seventh child. In that way, he got the House of Commons to pass the act. Later, when the usefulness of the family allowances was well established, the same government brought about the necessary changes, in order to give to the parents family allowances for every one of their children, whatever their number. Most certainly they have changed; at the time I am speaking about, the father of the hon. friend who has just interrupted me also worked on a farm, with equipment similar to mine. In my youth, however, people were not up to their necks in business, as my hon. friend is today.
Today, Mr. Chairman, I should like to make reference to the pensions for disabled persons. I am of those who believe that the regulations under which a person is judged eligible for the pension for disabled persons should be considered seriously by the provincial governments in order to remedy the 28902-5-320
Supply-Health and Welfare present situation that a person has to be practically or completely helpless to fulfil the requirements.
For instance, I have in mind the case of epileptics. It is also recognized that some other ailments represent a continuous danger for the employer and the employee. But those people have a right to live like anybody else and, indeed, it is enough to be affected by an ailment or a handicap without also being deprived of the benefits of the disabled persons pensions act.
Therefore, I urge the minister to take advantage of the conference soon to be held to conclude an agreement with the provinces so that those requirements may be mitigated and so that the granting of pensions under the Disabled Persons Act for those people who cannot work but who certainly have a right to live may be facilitated.
Before concluding, Mr. Chairman, I hope that this government will find a way to correct the situation I just mentioned in order to mitigate the requirements in regard to the disabled persons pensions. I am also convinced that this government will find a way, in due time, to extend family allowances to the age of 18, if not further, in the case of children still going to school and, providing the economy of the country permits, to give back to family allowances the purpose for which they were set up in 1945 by a Liberal government.

Mr. Chairman, I know we are all anxious to pass these estimates this evening if at all possible, and I can promise at the outset that I am not going to take up very much time in what I have to say tonight. I do wish, however, to take this opportunity to congratulate the minister on her appointment. While she may not have the most spectacular portfolio in the cabinet, or may not be dealing in astronomical figures which add up to billion dollar deficits, or may not be dealing with fantastic nuclear weapons or intercontinental missiles, she is dealing with the health of every man, every woman and every child in this country, and in my opinion she has one of the most remarkable portfolios in the cabinet. In addition to that, I must not overlook the fact that she is dealing with the finest profession in the world, the medical profession. I have every confidence that with her personality and great propensity for the truth she will not only carry on the work of this department but will add to and advance the great work it has carried out in the past and in recent years.
There have been great developments in this department in recent years, but we must

Supply-Health and Welfare realize that it also has problems. There are big problems in the department; there are big financial problems and there will be greater financial problems. The outlay of the department does not reap any obvious dividends in financial returns, but it results in dividends in the health, happiness and welfare of the people of our country. These dividends cannot be estimated in simple financial returns. There is the problem of great scientific developments, which must be given careful consideration in every way by the department. This is no time for smugness because of the fact that this department has operated so well; and I hope and am sure that it will continue to operate well in the future. This is the time for us to look for greater progress and greater developments in this wonderful department.
As we all know, Mr. Chairman, there are two definite aspects of this department. There is the welfare department and there is the health department. It is difficult to know just where one stops and the other begins because they are so completely in the same field, that of the welfare of our people. I will not spend much time dealing with the department of welfare because it has been adequately dealt with by other speakers. However, I do want to say that in general I endorse all the welfare programs that are carried on at the present time, and I know there will be more that I will be able to endorse in the future. I recognize, however-as I think everyone in this house recognizes-that there are still many deficiencies in the department of welfare; there are many abuses of the privileges offered by this department. We must also recognize the fact that there must be improvements and adjustments as far as possible to overcome some of these deficiencies.
In regard to the health aspect of the department, Mr. Chairman, I know the question of hospital insurance was adequately dealt with by the previous government. This program was in operation for many years in at least two provinces before the present federal government saw fit to introduce it on a national scale. I congratulate the previous government for introducing this scheme, which I know has been of great benefit to the provinces in the institution of hospital programs throughout Canada. Hospital care is, without question, a most demanding field. I wish to draw to the attention of the minister the fact that with advancing treatments and methods the need for hospital subsidization in the future will increase, and increase rapidly. I see no hope of avoiding increasing expenditure in the field of hospital care. Scientific developments, advanced treatments and every field of medicine have meant that hospital 

treatment is becoming the only efficient treatment, and home care is rapidly becoming less and less. This trend will continue. The patient is recovering much more quickly because he is receiving better treatment, and I think it should also be emphasized that in hospital the patient develops a psychological attitude that is a wonderful asset in his treatment and recovery. This attitude results from the fact that patients do not face the fear of a large hospital bill at the end of their treatment. In the field of health we face the problem of an increase in life expectancy. I think the minister should consider very seriously this increase in life expectancy. This has resulted from better sanitation, better preventive medicine and better medical care. I have not the figures before me but I think I am giving a conservative estimate when I say that in the last generation our life expectancy has increased by about ten years. This means that we are entering the field of geriatrics, and the Department of National Health and Welfare will be faced with the problem of providing increased subsidies for the treatment of the aged. We must have more care for those who will be confined to homes for the aged. We must have increased subsidies for those who are going to be confined to nursing homes. At the present time I think that the subsidy provided for nursing homes by both the provincial and federal governments is much too low.
Now, what can we expect in the future, Mr. Chairman? I know the question of health insurance has been mentioned briefly here tonight. During the last election campaign this government promised that we would have an insurance plan as soon as they took office. However, I noticed this item was lacking from the speech from the throne. I realize this program is not something one should rush into as the government has rushed into some of the ill-conceived programs presented this session. I hope that this measure will receive considerable study before anything further is advanced.
I should like to try to dispel right here, once and for all, the idea that the so-called orthodox medical men, to whom reference has been made this evening, are against such a program. We accept the principle that health insurance is a good thing for the country and a good thing for the people, if it is a proper health plan. Now, what do we mean by a health insurance scheme? I know that in so far as the people of British Columbia are concerned, about 80 per cent are covered by a satisfactory private health scheme. Then, there are the people who are on social welfare who are covered; but there are about 20 per cent who have no coverage. This is the group that needs coverage. This 20 per cent, probably because they are not indigent and

therefore not on welfare, are not able to pay for proper medical services. I do not consider for one minute that it is necessary for the government to undertake complete medical coverage as long as the private schemes are satisfactory. I do feel there is a group in our population that requires government assistance. I know the medical profession is in favour of that.
I believe that at the present time the majority of people are satisfied with their private schemes. We must remember that there must be no compulsion on anyone to enter a medical scheme. There are people who, for different personal reasons, religious reasons or other reasons should not be asked to contribute to a medical scheme if they do not want to come under it. We have to give a certain amount of leeway to these people, and we should devise a scheme that will be satisfactory to them. We must have a scheme that is going to be satisfactory not only to the medical profession but to the people who will be covered by it. The people must have a free choice of doctor. The doctors must be paid for services rendered and, except in the case of those working for institutions, they should not be put on a salary basis. There must be no directives to hospitals, except in the case of hospitals financed by the government.
I come now to what I consider to be the most important part of my remarks-and I do not believe this point has been mentioned by previous speakers. I refer to the necessity for research. Never in the history of our country has it been so important for us to consider seriously the matter of research. Research is a great benefit to everyone; it is of benefit to the people who are affected and to the medical profession. It is important to the economic welfare of our country. Canadians are recognized everywhere in the world for their high professional standards. They are considered to be industrious people who work well wherever they may go. The result is that Canadian scientists are very much in demand throughout the world. I do not mean to indicate we should in any way discourage our people from going to other countries to study and get new ideas; I believe this should be encouraged in every way possible. However, we must make it worth while for these same people to come back to our country.
Over the last 15 years or so this country has been losing medical men at the rate of about 250 per year. This means that about five medical men per week are going to the United States alone. In so far as the nursing profession is concerned, the statistics present an even worse picture. Fortunately, however, 28902-5-320J
Supply-Health and Welfare some of these people return to Canada. There is a loyalty to their country that brings them back. When they do come back they bring increased knowledge and increased training to this country, which has cost Canada nothing. However, we must make it worth their while to return to Canada. It is for this reason I say research is important. Some of these people stay in the United States for personal reasons, some of them like the climate and some of them like to make 50 per cent to 100 per cent more than they would in this country. The most important thing is that there are better job opportunities in the United States, better research facilities and they have better working conditions. These scientists are more appreciated in the United States than they are in Canada. We have to make it more worth their while to come back to this country.
We have had good research performed in this country, some of it under very unfortunate circumstances. I had the privilege of personal acquaintanceship with Dr. Fred Banting and Dr. Best and I know that the conditions under which they worked in making that important discovery of insulin were a disgrace to our country. Of course, the situation has improved since then, but we have a long way to go yet, Mr. Chairman. I must congratulate the department for its recognition in the last few years of the need for more research. The figures I received today indicated that in 1956-57 the department was appropriating $1,729,700 for medical research in Canada. I am glad to say that last year this amount was doubled, and I ask the minister to see that this branch receives more encouragement. We have the men and women in this country. We have the facilities; so by increasing our subsidies we can do much work in Canada and we can make Canada one of the greatest medical centres in the world.
In spite of the problems we have at the present time in the field of scientific research we have put up a very creditable performance in some of our hospitals and laboratories. Let us find a way to increase this research, to discover the mysterious diseases with which some of us are afflicted today. Let us show the minister why cancer of the lung may develop when we smoke too much. I am sure that every one of us is interested in research, and I know we can do more in this field in Canada. There has never before been a time when we faced so many problems in research as we do today, and I feel this is the place where more can be done than it can anywhere else. By this research we can prevent illness, save suffering and cut down on hospitalization. This has been reduced considerably.

One of the most important developments due to research work has been in the treatment of tuberculosis. Many tuberculosis institutions have been closed up now, and this has saved money for the country. This illustrates that we can save money by spending it in the proper way in the research branch of our national health and welfare department of the government. I urge the government at this time to advance further this most important department. The rewards will be great, not only for the welfare of our country but for our economy as well.

Mr. Chairman, following the example of the previous speaker, I do not intend to take much of the time of the house to deal with the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
By the way, I wish to congratulate the minister (Miss LaMarsh) for her appointment as head of one of the most important departments. In fact, last week, at the time of the introduction of the said estimates, it was repeated again and again that this department was second in importance. However, if you study the budget for the financial year ending March 31, 1964, you will find there is a correction to be made, for the estimates of the Department of National Defence for the financial year ending March 31, 1964 amount, approximately, to $1,619 million and those of the Department of Finance, to $1,302 million. Now, as the estimates for the Department of National Health and Welfare amount to $1,204 million, it comes third, and I believe it is normal to make that correction.
Mr. Chairman, I am of the opinion it is very important to recognize the great principle that tomorrow's economy should be more and more distributive, since we live in a world that improves constantly in the field of science. In fact, the various discoveries give today easier access to material things, at least to the production of material things which meet the needs of the human race.
If we take into account the fact that 23 per cent of the budget for the financial year ending March 31, 1964 is devoted to the Department of National Health and Welfare, it must be recognized that this is very encouraging for the future, since health and sanitation are no doubt the things that should have priority.
Mr. Chairman, reference was made, a moment ago, to the fact that in today's world, it is high time that society, and more particularly labour classes, venture more and more into the field of social legislation.
In fact, we notice nowadays that upon reaching the age of 45, 48, 50 or 55, a man who has worked many years in a plant finds himself dismissed. Automation is taking over


from him and he is often unable to find work that would suit his physical capacities or his insufficient training. Thus, he finds himself in a most difficult position.
We also notice that a great number of our fellow citizens are still too young to benefit from old age pension and on the other hand, too old to receive family allowances. Nevertheless, they are left with heavy responsibilities with regard to the education of their children who have started rather advanced studies.
That is why I am of the opinion that it is most important to go farther in the field of social security, from the standpoint of hospital and health insurance, family allowances and old age pensions.
During the discussion of the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare, we heard a lot about health insurance and hospital insurance.
According to the budget estimates, federal grants for hospital insurance and general health amount to $436 million. That is the share of the federal government for its contribution to various health or hospital insurance plans, in co-operation with the provinces that already have their health or hospital insurance schemes, some of which include medical costs.
If we analyse carefully this amount of $436 million, we find that the federal government spends about $75 a year per family as its share in hospital insurance plans, while the provinces who have such a plan have to contribute the same amount.
That means that between $125 and $150 for each Canadian family are spent on health insurance and hospital insurance in some provinces.
Now, I believe that if the same amount could be given out to family heads, to single people or to the older people who do not live with their families any more, each one of our Canadian families could get from companies operating in that field an insurance policy in case of illness and another one which would guarantee the payment of a salary during the stay in hospital of the family breadwinner; and that could be done for premiums of $125 or $150 a year.
We now have a hospital insurance scheme for the workers which guarantees, upon payment of approximately $10 a month, the protection of the worker and his family; if one member of the family falls ill, he can be admitted to the hospital free of charge and chirurgical expenses and visits by the physician are reimbursed.
I feel we should study the possibility of setting up for Canada a similar health insurance plan.

Of course some might say: Those amounts will be spent for things other than those they should be used for.
I will reply that the Department of National Health and Welfare could distribute to heads of family cheques for an amount equivalent to the actual cost of hospital insurance, which could be cashed only by companies or organizations specialized in the field of protection and for nothing but hospital insurance. I think that would cost less and families would get better coverage. Moreover, in many cases, it would enable them to get the physician they want, because you know what usually happens with regard to hospital insurance: to be admitted to a hospital, you must first prove to some official that you are ill enough to deserve a reservation for a hospital bed.
Therefore, I believe that the future health insurance plan should be studied from that angle to see if it would not be advisable to change the scheme which is already in the planning stage and taking form in our own province in the field of health insurance.
There is another very important side to the activities of the Department of National Health and Welfare, that of family allowances.
I believe everyone knows that it was one of the Liberal party's great promises; on the other hand, during the recent election campaigns, all parties stressed the need to review and amend that legislation so that it would better suit today's needs.
A while ago, the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Habel) gave us the impression he wanted to look back upon the past, and he went back as far as 1919 to remind us how this house had voted the Family Allowances Act.
At that time, the cost of living was much lower than nowadays, Canada was enjoying prosperity thanks to wartime activities, a very large number of family heads were able to earn their livelihood easily and properly by holding a position of some kind in our country, which was in full development in 1945.
If we consider the situation in the last five or six years, we realize that everything justifies a revision as soon as possible of this highly social legislation we have in the Family Allowances Act.
Mr. Chairman, as I said a while ago, it is sometimes sad for a family head to know that he is too young to receive a pension and too old to take advantage of family allowances. The father of a son aged 18, 19 or 20, who sometimes had to make great sacrifices to enable him to continue his education, is often unable, because he has lost his job, to keep his son in college or technical school, where he would graduate in two or three years.
Supply-Health and Welfare
We must amend the Family Allowances Act in order to extend the period of eligibility, perhaps until the child has completed his studies.
I hope that these suggestions will receive careful consideration; moreover they are consistent with a policy accepted and advocated by all the candidates during the last two election campaigns, for the problem of social security, pensions and family allowances was made much of at that time.
We also find under item "unemployment assistance" a federal government contribution of $110 million for social assistance to the unemployed, the disabled recognized as such, and those unable to provide for their own needs. One hundred and ten million dollars for the federal contribution. If we add to that the contribution of the different provinces, we get a very impressive amount.
But if we scrutinize the implementation of that legislation, we find that it is done with stinginess and even with discrimination.
Recently some of my constituents made certain representations to me concerning one of their fellow citizens who had benefited for nine years from the legislation for the blind and who, owing to obscure circumstances, after the last two elections, completely lost his claim to that pension in September 1963. In spite of representations which were made by both he and the head of his parish, the officials concerned seem to think that blindness is no longer a problem for him and that his eyesight is perfect. Yet, an optician who examined him told me personally: "That man will never recover sufficient eyesight to hold any kind of a job in industry or elsewhere." That is only one case out of hundreds.
I wonder if we should not also take a new approach to the distribution of purchasing power.
Last week the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) seemed to refer to a speech made by the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) in 1947. I feel we should have allowed him to continue his remarks because, in 1947, there was some talk about the national dividend and the distribution of our country's great wealth under the form of purchasing power. In my opinion, if that suggestion had been accepted, we would have fairly ridden Canada of all such cases of stinginess and discrimination.
In the field of national health, Mr. Chairman, we must concern ourselves mostly with the welfare of those who need not only medical care but also a sufficient quantity of calorie-rich food to sustain them so that they may not need medical attention too soon.
Let us think of the 500,000 to 600,00 Canadians who, over the past 26 years, have

Supply-Health and Welfare known the hardship which comes with unemployment. We could have increased consumption through a better distribution of the purchasing power, through increases in family allowances and old age pensions, and also by reducing the eligible age.
This would have been a real step towards social security which the people need more and more, like all human beings living in developed countries where scientific progress has taken place in the last 50 years.
I think that it is only natural that people are eager for security.
For the people in lower income groups who do not always get a hard-earned salary, because of unemployment, all this is very important.
I believe that all fields of social security should be examined during the discussion of the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare and that higher family allowances and for older children should be considered.
There is another field which, in my opinion, should be considered by the Department of National Health and Welfare, in co-operation with other departments if necessary, especially with provincial representatives, I mean amateur sport in the country.
We have in our province as well as in the others, various organizations, interested for example, in playgrounds and parish halls. I think that we should devote over $5 million to amateur sport. This higher grant should not solely be used to finance advanced studies, but should also be used for the improvement of instructors or other persons assigned to the organization of sport.
I think consideration should also be given to the advisability of a more active participation by the federal government and its closer co-operation with the provincial departments Of welfare and youth in order to grant subsidies to already existing bodies.
I gave as an example the playgrounds association, the O.T.J. of the province of Quebec. I know that there are in the other provinces across Canada similar organizations interested in athletics but what I have in mind, is a training program in physical fitness to give our youth a sound mind in a sound body. Our older citizens must facilitate the access to organized games and promote the physical development of our youngsters who represent the future of our nation.
That is why I think that in the field of amateur sport, the Minister of National Health and Welfare could certainly make a contribution to the development of a brighter future for our youth in terms of national health. We must not forget that national health is a
(Mr. Perron.]
matter of prime importance in modern societies and that the future belongs to the fighting man who has faith in the future.
It is our duty to anticipate what tomorrow will be and to do that, we must give today to our youth the best of health because insecurity holds nothing good in the heart of the underprivileged and insecurity is too often the lot of our large families either in the farming or working class.
In my constituency, hundreds of families live on farms with an income utterly inadequate which does not even allow them to get the bare necessities of life.
In fact, it was proven that 97,000 farms in eastern Canada have an annual income of less than $1,200 a year.
I think that the Minister of National Health and Welfare should take under serious consideration a way to supplement those completely inadequate incomes by increasing family allowances, if we wish to avoid the worst for those for whom the future holds in store nothing but misery for them and their dependents. I can assure you that it is sometimes very difficult to prevent people from considering that the wealthy should share their possessions with them.
We all want to take steps to make sure that in this country, the homes of those who are afflicted with illness and social insecurity will at last find happiness of some kind.
I think that it is up to the Department of National Health and Welfare to take up the challenge in connection with our future and to devise a program capable of ensuring security for the majority of our citizens, for in a country endowed with enormous riches of all kinds, we must assume the responsibility of solving this problem by pushing back as far as possible the frontiers of destitution and disease.
I believe that we live in a providentially privileged country in this regard. We have well organized political structures and, in my opinion, with the co-operation of the Minister of Finance, the Minister of National Health and Welfare will be able to find a way to get all the money needed to accelerate the increase in family allowances and the improvement of the old age pension scheme by lowering the age limit at which they become payable. Thus, a more prosperous and a more promising future will be in store for us.
