Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a few observations on these very important estimates which provide for the expenditure of over $1,200 million. I am one who believes that federal-provincial conferences that will deal particularly with problems relating to our human and natural

resources will be the foundation upon which we will build national unity in this country. I am convinced that the discussion of these practical things relating to human beings and the development of our natural resources in these conferences will bring about a great deal of understanding, and I think that has already been demonstrated to some extent by the conference of ministers on resources. I trust that all involved in the coming federal-provincial conference will reach agreement and come to conclusions that will be to the advantage of all the Canadian people, regardless of the province in which they live.
I want to extend my sincere congratulations to the minister on her appointment. I remember when she first came to the house as a neophyte, shall I say, on the opposition benches. It was not very long before she demonstrated by her debating ability, her vigour and her activity that she had a contribution to make to the house. In addition, she was the first lady member of the standing committee on veterans affairs. I do not know what some of the old boys I served with in the first world war would have said if they had known that veterans would wear petticoats in years to come. Anyway, it is a sign of the times, and she was very interested in veterans affairs. I wish her every success in the administration of her department and all she undertakes to the advantage of the people of Canada. I am sure she will not be content to be the ornamental apex of the broadly based department she administers.
I also wish to pay my tribute to the staff of the department both in Ottawa and in other places. I have had occasion to inquire about problems relating to senior citizens, medical questions and things of that sort, and so far as I am concerned I must say that the officials have taken every trouble to provide the information, although sometimes it is not easy to collate all the information some people seek. I have been here a good number of years, Mr. Chairman, and I cannot let the estimates of this department pass without making reference to the contribution to the department and to the Canadian people that the lady secretary of the department has made throughout the years.
I am not going to waste the time of the house by repetition, but in a sentence or two I do want to support the pleas made by previous speakers for the establishment of a national health insurance plan, something that this party has been urging for years. We hope that the developments that will occur in connection with the pension plan, and the developments that have occurred in some of the provinces in this connection, will spur the government on to take the bull by the horns,
Supply-Health and Welfare as it were, and give some leadership in connection with a national health insurance plan.
I want to say a word or two about welfare before going on with my other remarks. I remember the welfare that existed when I was a boy. It was known as parish relief. If you were down and out and almost starving you could go to the workhouse. If you were able-bodied you worked on a pile of stones splitting flints that were crushed into the macadam roads of Great Britain. This was the way welfare was administered, and the situation was very similar in this country in the early days as far as the meagreness of welfare is concerned.
We have come a long way since then. Now we are in most unusual circumstances compared with years ago. We find that the majority of people in Canada, including the rich and the poor, now support the welfare state. But these people support the welfare state from two different motives. I have talked to prominent industrialists who expressed their support for all types of welfare legislation. You will find them acting as officers of welfare concerns, local committees, and so on. While in some cases there is a touch of hu-manitarianism in this, I have talked to some of these people who considered it was good business. They can pay welfare benefits today that they could not years ago, and all because of increased production. They consider it is really good insurance against social revolution, and also for the maintenance of the capitalist system.
In that connection I want to quote briefly from Maclean's magazine, October 6, 1942, which had a very interesting article dealing with developments with respect to the former government. On page 76 I read this:
Nothing in this classically competitive business history would lead you to suppose that some of McCutcheon's ideas might alarm a dogmatic capitalist, but such is the surprising case. A caption in the Toronto Star of September 30, 1957, read: "Praises Canada's drift toward welfare state.''
Just imagine a multi-millionaire making a statement like that 25 or 30 years ago. He would have been kicked out of the establishment.
The account of a speech McCutcheon had made to the Canadian club followed. "Relating.. .the vast expansion of government and voluntary health and welfare programs, (McCutcheon) said. 'You might expect me as a businessman to denounce this whole movement.. .as a dangerous if not to say pernicious thing. On the contrary. I regard it not only as one of the greatest achievements of private enterprise and a modern industrial society. I consider it necessary to the continued existence of both.' "
That is the point of view of many of the wealthier people who support welfare at this time. Mr. Chairman, my colleague says I mentioned 1942. I misread the date; it is 1962. Of course my colleague is very fond of exactitude in small matters.

Supply-Health and Welfare
Now, Mr. Chairman, that is not our point of view. We look upon the welfare state as paving the highway to social justice for everyone, and not as causing some people to suffer in perpetuity human indignity by being kept on welfare in the sense of the persons I have mentioned. We mean that the welfare state should provide for every child in the country, regardless of place of birth or economic circumstances of the parents. We believe that all able-bodied men should be provided with employment at decent wages and in proper working conditions. We believe that all Canadians are entitled to decent housing, and to protection by national welfare against the hazards of ill health. We believe that our aging citizens are entitled to retire in comfort with a measure of security. We do not look upon this as subsidizing human beings to stay on the shelf because they are no longer of use in the society in which we live. We believe in human dignity and opportunities for all according to their physical and intellectual development.
I listened with interest to the speech made by the hon. member who represents Kamloops. He is a member of the medical profession, and I heard with particular interest his references to the need for greater research in many aspects of health and welfare. I heartily support those remarks. I do not intend to repeat them but I have had this brought to my attention by persons in my own constituency, by local groups interested in the problem of rehabilitation, particularly of children and juveniles, and I support their pleas for wider, more expanded research into all aspects and all problems relating to the development of a sound policy within this department.
I now want to say a few words about the pension plan. Our hopes were raised very high during the election period, and we came here with great expectations and anticipations. Because of circumstances that have developed this delay has occurred; however, as a result of this forthcoming conference I hope this will provide an opportunity to develop a sound plan related to the circumstances of the times.
I fully appreciate the opposition the government has received from some quarters to a national contributory pension plan. I am not sure whether I should have said that, or whether I should have said a confederation contributory pension plan. Anyway, you know what 1 mean. Mr. Chairman, my colleague is again correcting me in matters of minutiae: It is the Canada pension plan. There is nothing like having a prompter behind the wings. He should have been on the stage, or behind the back door but out of sight.
[Mr. Herridge.l

Anyway, we all know there has been strong opposition, and I want to give credit to the minister for the stand she is taking in placing the broad outline before the house in the form of a resolution, and not backing down one iota. She is not given to easily changing direction because of the zephyrs slight political winds and things of that sort, and we wish her well in standing her ground.
In that connection I would like to quote a cutting sent to me by some of my constituents who are interested in this question. It is an editorial from the Star Weekly of recent issue. It is well worth reading into the record, because in my opinion the person who wrote the editorial sized the situation up very well indeed. It is headed, "Big finance fights pensions"-we all agree with that-and states:
Powerful interests have begun a mighty lobbying campaign against the Canada pension plan now before parliament. They are the insurance and trust companies which control the huge funds built up under private pension plans.
The Canada pension plan offers more, to more Canadians, than any private plan or any combination of private plans can give them. It will cover almost every employed worker in Canada unless he lives in a province that stays out, as Quebec will.
According to this editorial.
After it has been in effect 10 years it will pay a man aged 70, who has been earning $77 a week, a pension of $175 a month. This is a far quicker build-up to maximum than private plans, which might take 40 years to reach this point.
Some of what the insurance interests are saying is plain hogwash.
That is a rather plain word.
"Canada is looking into the jaws of an economic catastrophe," says one document. Others use more skilful arguments and figures. Among the main points the insurance men attack are:
The cost. Contributions from worker and employer will not exceed 2 per cent of wages (up to $77 a week) for the first 10 years, then will increase. Government actuaries have worked this out extremely carefully, allowing for the proportion of old people there may be in the population.
Very fairly they give both a high cost and a low cost. In the year 2050, for instance, they reckon that, on optimistic assumptions, the plan will cost only 4.38 per cent of wages. But on a pessimistic basis they say it might cost 8.84 per cent.
Opponents have immediately seized on the highest figure and some even say, without giving any facts, that the cost will really be much higher.
How much pension? Insurance men say the plan "overpensions" people.
Isn't that a frightful cry-they actually overpay pensioned people. To talk of giving our older citizens some measure of comfort is absolutely atrocious in their point of view.
Even with an extra $75 of old age pension for a wife, a couple will have only $250 a month at most. Many will have less if they retire early or don't earn as much as $77 a week when working. Is this too much pension?
Pay as you go. The argument against this part of the plan is that because it pays pensions out of contributions as it receives them, it is destroying an important part of our savings system.

That is an insurance company's point of view. They have been collecting the savings, keeping the profits and investing them wherever they saw fit, without any thought being given to the best advantage of the development of this country, and in some cases investing them in foreign companies to quite an extent.
The building up of funds under private plans provides money for businesses to expand and helps the country to grow, this argument goes.
What the Canada pension plan's opponents do not say is that the United States has had a similar pension scheme since 1937 and that there private pension plans have gone on growing alongside it and providing billions of dollars for investment. There's no reason why this shouldn't happen here too.
Then, as a clincher, the insurance men ask that the plan be delayed so there can be full discussion on it. We believe that its details should be carefully checked, possibly by the House of Commons banking committee. Now that it is proposed to bring the present $65 old age pension up to $75 without waiting for the Canada pension plan, an extra two months' delay won't do any harm, and a lot of improvements may be made in that time.
What the big financial interests fighting the plan want is not just delay. They hope to kill it dead. In the interests of security and decent comfort for our old people at the end of their working days, parliament must thwart their design and establish the Canada pension plan.
I give full credit to the editorial writer of the Star Weekly who wrote that article. He has done a service to Canada to state the situation in such clearcut language. As I said before, I trust that the coming conference will bear good fruit in respect to this pension plan, and once again I wish the minister, the other members of the cabinet and the officials attending the conference every success in their negotiations in this respect.
Now I want to say a few words about the Disabled Persons Act. I am trying to be as brief as possible, Mr. Chairman, but it is very difficult for me to get the floor on some occasions. In the first place, I am a modest person-

Mr. Chairman, I welcome this opportunity of speaking a second time on the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare as I have two thoughts that I would like to advance, both of which I think are for the national good, under the headings of health and welfare. First I should emphasize that I am a nonsmoker. I have not indulged in the habit since corn tassels and toilet paper went out of style. When I say toilet paper, that was in the days before Facelle toilet tissues were made in my riding of York-Humber-and I mean toilet paper. I thought the habit rather disgusting at that time and have never taken it up. As a non-smoker I would like to urge that this conference on Monday and Tuesday be thrown open to the public and the press. I sincerely believe that the more publicity there is given to this conference, the more effect it will have on the young people of the nation and it will influence many of them to not take up the habit.
I have been 40 years in the newspaper business and I know how much attention is paid by newspapers and periodicals to a mere press hand-out from a conference held behind closed doors. If the conference is in the open, the press, radio, and possibly television, will give it wide coverage and the import of the deliberations will be broadcast from coast to coast. I would like to see the conference given as widespread publicity as possible.
Having incurred the askance looks of my hon. friends from Norfolk and Durham, where tobacco is grown in large quantity, because I favour publicity that may retard this habit, I would point out that I have a large number of variety stores in the riding of York-Humber which could take offence at my remarks, and I would now like to make an effort to placate them. I am a non-smoker and I am in this House of Commons a great deal for the simple reason that I do not find it necessary to go behind the curtains from time to time or go into the members' lobby, nor do I walk around the parliament buildings, in order to indulge in the habit of courting lady nicotine. We have certain members of the press gallery who are here a minimum of time, possibly 30 [Mr. Herridge.l
minutes a day, who retreat to their warrens on the third floor and write lengthy articles pointing out the terrible attendance of the members of the House of Commons. But they do not point out when they are writing those articles that they themselves are not in the House of Commons, and they do not give the members of the house credit for leaving the chamber for the same reason they leave the press gallery, namely to work in their offices or to smoke in various places and various postures.
I would point out that when I came into this chamber this evening I counted the number of Liberals sitting in the members' lobby and I would report to you, not with any great degree of pleasure, that there were almost as many members in the members' lobby or behind the curtains enjoying themselves, under the heading of "welfare", as there were in this chamber. This is a small item of news for the hon. member for Grey-Bruce, if he wishes to know where we are most of the time.
I should like to make this suggestion in all seriousness, bearing in mind the fact that I personally am not addicted to this habit of smoking, that you would have double the attendance in this chamber after orders of the day if smoking were permitted here. Some newspapers are keeping box scores relating to members' attendance in the house. I have a better than average figure because I do not smoke and I am in the house a great deal. Many members go out to smoke. I do have a tremendous number of friends who indulge in the filthy habit and I do not think any worse of them than I do of my friends, like the hon. member for Niagara Falls or the hon. member for York West, who set a non-smoking example which all members do not always follow. We would like to have smoking allowed in the House of Commons so that a large number of members would come in here and see the example set by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the hon. member for York West and the hon. member for York-Humber, and then they might come to the conclusion they must give up smoking following the realization that lung cancer is staring them in the face.

Having heard this rather humorous dissertation, Mr. Chairman, I am wondering if my somewhat sober remarks will be listened to at all. Actually, after the comments made by these speakers this evening, I would think the minister, as head of the department, would realize that her estimates could not be reduced because each speaker has advocated an increase in the various programs that have been discussed. I am thinking of disabled persons allowances, and

so on, which it has been advocated should be increased. Actually, I can support this myself.
Various references have been made to the health insurance plan. It was rather a curious experience to hear an hon. member opposite- I cannot recall his constituency-speak in favour of health insurance and speak also in favour of proceeding slowly. During the election campaign, this was one of the things that was promised immediately. We were told we would have this plan as soon as the Liberals took power. It is not necessary for me to remind the committee that our party is not opposed to medical insurance. In fact, it was our party that initiated the commission, under Dr. Hall, to study the whole question of health services. This would be the basis for an adequate study of any program of insurance. I think this is certainly a very sensible approach to this vast problem.
In introducing the estimates the minister stated that better than 19 per cent of the federal budget is required for health and welfare. I think translated into other terms this statement speaks of the high quality of services the Canadian people receive from this significant department. When I recall that this department has not yet existed for 20 years and has already reached the point of requiring such a share of the total expenditure, I must compliment the minister on accomplishing this degree of service to Canadians.
I noticed in the estimates provision has been made for an increase in welfare grants. I was interested in the cumulative spending for research, welfare grants and health grants. The whole grants program of this department is a great thing. While the amount in the estimates has been increased from $250,000 to $500,000, I think in this present day and age, when it can be said that 90 per cent of the scientists who ever lived are still alive, and when the statement is made that knowledge doubles itself almost every ten years, the government needs to recognize that there has to be some impetus, some encouragement given to the development of better trained personnel. This is especially true at a time when the cost of higher education seems to be increasing as well. I would admonish the minister to give thought to an even greater increase in the grants program.
Mention has been made of the pension plan. It is a source of some sadness to me that the plan had to be introduced in such great haste and therefore has now had to be shelved, at least temporarily. I, personally, and I think most members of the house, are in favour of a pension plan that has been solidly conceived and one that will be workable, because there are many individuals who are not 28902-5-321J
Supply-Health and Welfare covered by private programs about which we hear so much. There is one theory advanced that would solve our whole problem in this area, and that is that as long as the economy increases at the rate it has, and the productivity keeps increasing at the present rate, the standard of living of Canadians will be doubled in one generaion, or 30 years. In this way, the problem of welfare would more or less resolve itself. If this were so, it would lead to the rather tempting solution of simply sitting and waiting until the economy of the country reached this point.
Of course, this is not possible, nor could it be. I was, therefore, reassured when the minister said in introducing these estimates that we would, of course, have to spend whatever is necessary to assure Canadians of the highest possible standard of health. She assured the committee that there would be no skimping in this area. I am reassured by this kind of statement because I feel in the years to come the department will really enlarge its expenditures as it will its services. All studies indicate that the theoretical possibility of the poor disappearing, through this formula I just mentioned of the standard of living doubling, does not work. If you do some reading in this field, I would refer you to studies made in the United States, a country which claims the average level of income per family is something like $7,000 per year. In spite of this rather high level of income, it is still possible to speak of the mass phenomena of the poor in that country. There have been many books written on this subject, but I would like to refer to the book written by Mr. Michael Harrington which he calls, "The Other America; Poverty in the United States". This certainly points up that this faceless group has no real representative in our society.
Just where to draw the poverty line in Canada is something I would not want to undertake at this time because so many things have to be considered. According to a recent census, over half of our single persons earn less than $2,000 per year. If you want to apply this to families, I think the figures show that something like 40 per cent of the families earn less than $4,000 per year. Now, whether we can consider this to be the poverty line or not, I am not too sure. I put it to the members of the house to try to establish just where we would be in attempting to provide the many needs of our families if we had only $4,000 to buy education, to buy clothing, shelter and the many other things a family requires. I say, therefore, that a great awakening of the public conscience is necessary to the fact that we are far from

Supply-Health and Welfare an affluent society, in spite of the fact we enjoy one of the highest standards of living in the world.
If we live in the suburbs, I believe it is quite easy to be convinced that we do, in fact, live in an affluent society because the poor have a way of disappearing. They are confined in crowded, miserable housing in the centre of town and many of us hardly even notice them.
Another reason they are becoming invisible Is because many of them are at an age where they are quite isolated from the rest. Some are over 65 years of age and the dependants of those families with limited incomes to which I referred are under 18 years of age. These groups are not very vocal in our society, yet most of the services of the department are directed at them. The book to which I referred, "The Other America" by Michael Harrington, has this comment:
And finally the poor are politically invisible... They are without lobbies of their own; they put forward no legislative program. As a group they are atomized; they have no face, they have no voice.
One of the biggest causes of poverty, I suggest, is unemployment. We know that much of the complexity of this problem of unemployment cannot be blamed entirely on the lack of government programs, although the government shoulders a heavy responsibility to provide increasing opportunities for employment. But it seems that the human race no longer fits society. Here I should like to quote from the September 1962 issue of Harper's magazine, an article entitled "The Stupidity Problem"-an odd term-by Mr. John Fischer:
The human race-or anyhow that sample of it located in North America-no longer fits the kind of society it has to live in. Our society just does not have any jobs for certain people. If it continues to develop along its present course, the numbers of such unemployables seem likely to grow rather rapidly.
Then he goes on to outline the difficulty of finding employment for all, especially those less adequately suited for the complex jobs of today. Then he concludes with this comment:
For we have apparently built ourselves unintentionally, and without realizing it, a society which calls for a distribution of intelligence entirely different from that which God provided. It remains to be seen whether we can make it work.
Indeed, all the resources of health and welfare, of housing, education and employment, will have to be applied to see whether we can really make our society work.
Why do I show concern in this area? How well have we done up to now? I should like to use educational achievements as some sort of measure. If it is said that this is not really a proper yardstick to use when discussing
[Mr. Enns.l
the estimates of the department of health and welfare, I suggest that education is very much tied in with health and welfare. For example, how many of us know that more than 200,000 adults in Canada have never gone to school? Do we realize, Mr. Chairman, the employment problems facing this group? Some 870,000 Canadians did not get past grade four. There are other figures to show that 70 per cent of unemployed men at the present time have no more than grade eight education. The national employment service tells us that if you have not at least grade eight education you are ineligible for more than 70 per cent of the jobs available. Finally, there are something over 7 million Canadians who have never completed high school. When we look at the various qualifications now expected even of office boys, where it seems matriculation is mandatory, we can see the complexity of the problem which faces anyone who attempts to find a solution to the unemployment question.
Obviously we have failed somewhere along the line. One of the chief reasons is that we look too closely and too critically at the cost of health services, at the cost of welfare services, and at the cost of education, while ignoring the fact that the cost of failing to spend money to provide adequate health, welfare and education services is much greater. What is the cost of unemployment, for example? What of the frustration of the people who cannot find work? What about the enforced idleness, the loss of purpose and selfrespect, or even the loss of hope and faith? There are even more tangible indicators of the effects of unemployment, such as the loss of homes through mortgage foreclosures, development of delinquency, and I can name many others. In comparison the provision of welfare services, work projects and other measures to stimulate the economy is clearly a lesser price to pay. What about the cost of sickness, pain, suffering, chronic incapacity and loss of income owing to inadequate medical and health services? Society as a whole, as well as the individual who is ill, pays an enormous price for the burden of illness. Beside these costs the price of adequate health services is surely small. What about the cost of ignorance, of reduced job opportunities, frustration, long hours of drudgery, perhaps even unemployment, and even more important, failure in the fulfilment of life? If we are wise we will pay for health and welfare and adequate educational measures simply because we cannot afford ignorance, sickness and personal misery.
This leads me to three specific proposals I should like to put forward. One is in the area of health, and this is not a proposal which has not already been discussed. It advocates

the implementation of a properly thought out health insurance scheme. I read the report of the department for 1962-63 and was interested to see that something like 98.7 per cent of all Canadians are covered by hospitalization schemes. What a difference that is when compared with the less than 50 per cent who receive coverage through a medical insurance scheme at the present time. I say there is great need for a health insurance scheme which will be acceptable to the medical profession. It must be a scheme that will still be locally and regionally controlled, and various methods of financing must be well considered before it is put forward. I am looking to provinces like Saskatchewan, and Ontario which is contemplating a scheme, and also Alberta. I am hopeful that Canada will before long develop, in the same way it developed a workable hospitalization scheme, a health insurance scheme. I think it is unfair that medically indigent people are dependant on the charitable inclinations of the medical profession to provide adequate health services. In the area of welfare I look with some alarm at the complexity and diversity of the numerous schemes at the present time serving the people. For example, I think of the workmen's compensation act, veterans pensions, unemployment insurance, family allowances, mothers' allowances, disability allowance, allowances for the blind and disabled, and the various old age security pensions, veterans allowances and general assistance. Surely there must be a way of simplifying this maze of different programs jointly financed by federal money, provincial money, municipal money and voluntary schemes.
This leads me to advocate a social security plan which will funnel these individual programs into one scheme. The saving in administrative duplication would be considerable and the service to the entitled recipients would certainly be enhanced. I am hopeful that some of the recommendations of the Gill commission can be considered in the wider application and development of a social security program. So any social security program should be preceded by careful study of the conditions which exist under present provisions, before its implementation.
The third and last suggestion I wish to make has to do with education. I make it with reluctance because I do not wish to lay upon an active minister and upon a department which already has many diverse functions, yet another burden. Yet I feel there has to be a branch responsible for the field of education at a national level. We hear much talk about the need for granting scholarships, about increasing demands for university grants and the requirements of the vocational and
Supply-Health and Welfare technical training program. All this has to do with education. There is another problem which confronts many families, including particularly the families of service men and others in our society who are becoming less and less rooted. In many cases their children encounter setbacks, not because they lack ability but because they suddenly encounter a school curriculum or program which is completely different from anything they had been undertaking previously. For this reason I think a branch should be set up to deal with this aspect of the educational field and that the department should be renamed the department of health, welfare and education.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I did have a lengthy speech prepared on a number of topics but in view of the hour, and in an effort to co-operate with the minister, I will shorten my remarks as much as possible. The first thing I should like to bring to the hon. lady's attention is the question of blind pensions, disabled persons allowances and old age security payments. As a number of other members have mentioned, we hope that all those people in receipt of these payments will soon get the $10 increase. I hope the government will bring in legislation accordingly at an early date because these people badly need the extra allowance.
There is another matter I should like to bring to the attention of the committee. I know it has been discussed over the years in this chamber. I know it was being discussed ten years ago. It is the question of removing the means test as a condition of payment of pensions to the blind, and I think the minister should give careful attention to this principle not only as it applies to the blind but as it applies to disabled persons allowances. The application of the means test necessitates certain administrative expenditure and, in addition, it is embarrassing to a number of the applicants. People who are blind are deprived of a valuable physical asset when it comes to earning a living. Through no fault of their own they have probably not been able to make a living as well as the rest of us, and for this reason we should help them out by compensating them in some small way for the loss of a valuable physical asset. It is true a number of blind persons may be able to make a living, but they are not able to do so as well as if they had not lost their sight.
I feel that in all these cases an allowance should be granted without a means test being applied. I know there may be some who have lost their sight and who do not really need the allowance, but the same could be said in this particular respect of some of those in receipt of old age security benefits. The great majority do, and if payments are made to a

Supply-Health and Welfare few people who are affluent, it must be remembered that the money usually goes back in taxes, anyway. I understand that most blind persons in this country lost their sight at a very early period in their lives.
As far as the payment of disabled persons allowances is concerned, the same principle should apply, though we should perhaps bear in mind that these people may have become physically handicapped later in life and would therefore have had a better opportunity to earn a living than most blind persons. Perhaps, in these circumstances, a regulation could be made specifying that if the handicaps had occurred prior to the age of 35 the payment should be granted without a means test. In cases where the handicap was sustained beyond that age, the means test would continue to apply.
With regard to the disabled persons allowance, the hon. member for Kootenay West brought certain complaints to the attention of the minister and I want to re-emphasize what he had to say. Most members of this house have had case after case brought to their attention involving persons who are very ill, who cannot work, and who, in all probability, will never be able to work again. But when they apply for the allowance their applications are turned down because they are not considered to be totally and permanently disabled. Apparently, under the regulations as they now apply, if there is the remotest possibility that a person may be able to move again he is denied this type of allowance. I am sure this was never the intention when the legislation was passed. Possibly the situation has come about because of the way in which the regulations are enforced by the federal and provincial authorities concerned.
I hope the minister will give this situation a careful second look. I could mention dozens of cases of this kind which have come to my attention. These people are totally disabled, but they are told that because 15 years later they may possibly be able to walk again, the allowance cannot be granted. Then there are those who are permanently, but not totally disabled. A man might be able to work with his left hand. This is a kind of argument I have had brought to my notice time after time. The officials say: We would like to do something, but the regulations do not permit us. Once again, I suggest the minister give this situation her close attention.
I should like to turn briefly to consider what might be done with regard to a new type of food poisoning which has been in the news of late, an extremely rare type of poisoning known as botulism. There have been several instances of it lately and I hope the minister will consider advising the food and drugs division of her department to see

that warnings are passed to those who are processing food and to make sure a plentiful supply of antidote is available for the treatment of those who do contract this illness. The cause of this illness is a type of bacteria which occurs, I am told, in non-acid foods only, in the absence of oxygen, as, for example, when smoked fish is wrapped in cellophane and left for some time in storage. The unfortunate thing is that this type of food poisoning is not easy to avoid because the food affected is unchanged as to taste, odour and colour. People have no warning that they are eating contaminated food. I hope the department will do everything it can through education and publicity to make the public and others concerned aware of this problem. I hope, too, that it will keep a careful check on food processing plants, particularly those handling foods which are wrapped in cellophane and which may be stored for a while before they are used.
To turn to another subject, I wish the minister could give us a brief report, when she replies, as to the present situation with respect to the analysis of samples of radioactive materials which have been collected in Canada and around the world. I am sure she knows that a few years ago the United Nations was interested in a project of this sort. It still is, as I gathered when I was in attendance there not long ago. Samples of air, soil, water and food were collected by various countries. Canada offered to analyse these samples for countries which do not have facilities for doing so. Ghana, Burma, Pakistan and one or two other countries have sent samples to Canada to be analysed. The information is collated and sent to the United Nations so that we can keep track of radioactive fall-out in Canada and in other parts of the world. Maybe people think they know how long this material stays aloft after these explosions but we have all read reports of live material falling in large quantities in northern Canada and perhaps elsewhere, and we do not know how long it stays up. There have been a good many guesses but I understand nobody really knows how long it stays aloft, what happens to it when it comes down and in what concentration it does come down.
It is true there is a nuclear test ban treaty at the moment but one can never tell when the treaty might be broken. We hope it never will be. In any event, from previous tests in the atmosphere we know that this material is still coming down and we would like to know to what extent. I know we are supposed to be analysing samples from these other countries and I hope the minister can give us some information.

Finally, on the subject of tobacco I understand the minister is helping to convene a conference in Ottawa next week on cigarette smoking and the allegedly attendant evils. From all the information we have available it seems pretty clear that cigarette smoking does do some harm to people by causing some varieties of heart disease and arterial disease, and apparently it is a contributing factor in certain forms of lung cancer. I draw the minister's attention, as I am sure some of her colleagues already have, to the fact that the tobacco growing industry in Canada is a $100 million a year business. If basic research is not going on already in the laboratories that come under the minister's jurisdiction, I hope that some will be carried on to try to find what the agent is in cigarettes that may produce cancer, and if that agent can be found to exist then I hope some way of removing it can be devised. The industry is far too big a one to toss overboard without making some effort to save it. If there is some substance in cigarettes that causes cancer, let us try to find out what it is and try to find some way of removing it. I am sorry to take so much time but there were a number of points I wanted to bring to the minister's attention.

people who do not fall within this classification and therefore do not obtain an allowance. The regulations have been drawn as a result of consultation between the two levels of government.
However, I am informed that within the last few years many people who do not qualify as being completely and permanently disabled, qualify under unemployment assistance programs. They are not employable and therefore they receive some assistance.
As all hon. members know, there have been a number of questions asked within the last few weeks regarding the basic categorical programs. I have indicated, as has the Prime Minister, that because of the fact that this topic has been requested by the provinces as a matter for insertion in the agenda of the federal-provincial conference to commence on Monday, no action was being taken in concert with the old age security increases. The hon. member for Oxford raised a question with respect to collections of samples in various countries to count radioactive fallout as a result of United Nations resolution 1379, passed in 1959. I have very little information with me with respect to this, but I am informed some four countries negotiated with Canada in order that details of samples, types, procedures and frequencies might be developed. As a result, we are receiving regularly from Pakistan samples of milk and food products, and samples of soil from Burma. I have not got any other information available at the moment, but I will be glad to obtain it and supply it to my hon. friend.
With respect to the topic of a number of speeches, the family allowance increase, my hon. friends have also placed questions on the order paper and have been informed by myself and the Prime Minister that this is indeed a part of the program of the government, a program for parliament, and that in the priorities which were given by the government, this did not obtain the highest priority.

the report of the Hall commission is expected within a few months, and I should expect that taking any action without having that com-misison report before us would be precipitate.

subtopic: COMMUNIQUE ON MEETING OF O.E.C.D.

speechtext:
1.	The ministerial council of the O.E.C.D. held its annual meeting in Paris on 19th and 20th November, 1963, under the chairmanship of the Hon. Halvard Lange, minister for foreign affairs of Norway, and reviewed the economic prospects for its twenty member countries and their economic relations with the rest of the world.
2.	The prospects for economic growth in member countries are on the whole better than last year. The United States, the United Kingdom and Canada are now progressing at a faster rate. In other member countries expansion continues. In the expectation that this growth will be supported by suitable measures in the United States and other countries, the increase of the gross national product of the O.E.C.D. area as a whole for the years 1960-64 will probably correspond to the growth target of 50 per cent set for the decade of the 1960's by the first ministerial council in 1961.
The importance of internal stability for balanced economic growth was stressed. Costs and prices in a few European countries are rising rapidly. A stabilization plan is being put into effect in France. Measures have been taken in Italy; further steps must be envisaged.
3.	As regards international payments, measures undertaken by member countries, and the recent trends of trade among them, have begun and should continue progressively to create better equilibrium between the deficit and surplus countries. It is important that measures adopted by all member countries to deal with their internal economic situations should continue to take into account their effects on the general equilibrium of international payments.
4.	In member countries in the process of development, economic growth in recent years has generally been somewhat faster than in the O.E.C.D. area as a whole. However, it can hardly be said that the desirable narrowing of the gap between these and other member countries has really begun; much remains to be done.
The ministers considered it desirable, therefore, that the organization and its more developed members should continue to devote their attention and co-operation to the development problems of the less developed member countries.
Ministers noted with satisfaction that a new Spanish development program will be
inaugurated in 1964. The ministers also reviewed the situation of the consortia for aid to Greece and Turkey and reaffirmed the importance which they attached to the efforts of member countries in support of the development of these two countries, particularly by the provision of long term development capital on favourable terms.
5.	Ministers reviewed the work of the organization in the fields of agriculture, industry and manpower, and agreed that this work should increasingly be directed to the problems of adaptation arising from changes in the economics of member countries. They considered in particular that the organization should pursue its work on an active manpower policy, and on the retraining of manpower as well as on mobility of manpower and industry.
6.	Ministers noted with satisfaction the results of the ministerial meeting on policies for science and technology on 3rd and 4th October, 1963.
7.	The ministers noted that development aid has been maintained at a high level and on improved terms, although the earlier rate of increase has not continued. The needs of the developing countries are, however, increasing, and great problems lie ahead. Past results have depended largely on public support in member countries. The provision of aid to meet the expanding needs of the less developed countries will depend even more on such support in the future and will be related increasingly to measures of self help in the recipient countries.
The ministers emphasized the value of the confrontations of national aid programs through the organization, and asked members further to co-ordinate their efforts with a view to making aid more effective in response to priority needs in the less developed countries. They also welcomed the intention expressed by the members of the D.A.C. of relating more nearly the terms of aid to debt servicing capacities of recipients. Important steps had been taken by some members in this connection during the past year. Ministers noted the decline in private capital movements from the industrialised countries to the less developed countries and asked the organization to consider further what steps might be taken by industrialised and less developed countries to increase the flow.
The ministers welcomed the establishment of the O.E.C.D. development centre.

8.	Since last year's ministerial meeting, the organization has devoted a great deal of attention to the ways and means to increase the export earnings of less developed countries, member and non-member.
The bulk of the exports of the less developed countries still consists of primary products of which O.E.C.D. countries are the main importers. Various methods for stabilizing and increasing the export earnings from these commodities are now being studied. Ministers stressed the importance of this work. Member countries should join in efforts to improve the market conditions for primary products.
Increasingly, however, the less developed member and non-member countries need to diversify their economies and encourage the
production of manufactured articles for their own markets and for exports. The industrialised countries of the O.E.C.D. should facilitate this development by providing enlarged access to their markets for these products. The ministers noted with approval that full reciprocity from less developed countries was not being demanded for the tariff reductions expected from the forthcoming round of GATT tariff negotiations.
Ministers instructed the organization to continue work and consultations concerning the trade problems of the less developed countries.
They voiced the determination of their governments to prepare for the United Nations conference on trade and development in a constructive spirit.
